lessons.title: Two Little Hands

activities.prompt: What fun things can our hands and little body do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Little Hands
activities.body: Your body has many parts. Your hands clap. Your legs walk. Your eyes look around. Your ears hear any sound. Your nose smells and breathes. Your mouth likes to eat and talks. Your head moves. This little body belongs to you.
keyPoints: Hands clap and legs walk.
Eyes look and ears hear.
Nose smells and breathes; mouth eats and talks.
activities.explanation: Your body parts each do special things.

activities.prompt: At song time, the ears hear clapping. The child turns the head. Why?
steps: The ears hear any sound, so the child hears the clapping.
The eyes look around, so the child can look for the clapping.
The head moves, so the child can turn to look.
So the child turns the head to look for the clapping.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do your hands do?
activities.explanation: Hands clap to make a sound.

activities.prompt: Your ______ hear any sound.
activities.hint: They are on your head.
activities.explanation: Ears hear sounds all around you.

activities.prompt: Match each body part to what it does.
activities.explanation: Each body part has its own job.

activities.prompt: Which body part helps you smell and breathe?
activities.explanation: The nose helps you smell and breathe.

activities.prompt: What does the song have?
activities.explanation: The song has clapping and tapping.

activities.prompt: Match each action to the body part that does it.
activities.explanation: Different body parts do different actions.

activities.prompt: At song time, the song has clapping. The child wants to join the clapping. What will the child do?

Walking is for legs, so it does not join clapping.
Smelling is for the nose, so it does not join clapping.
Talking is for the mouth, so it does not join clapping.

activities.explanation: The song has clapping, so the hands clap to join.

activities.prompt: A sound is near the child. The ears hear it. What helps the child look for the sound?

The nose smells and the mouth eats, so it cannot help look.
The legs walk and hands clap, so this does not help look.
The mouth talks and ears hear, so this does not help look.

activities.explanation: The eyes look around and the head moves, so this helps look.

activities.prompt: The child talks. Then the child eats. Which body part does both?

The nose smells and breathes, so it does not do both.
The ears hear any sound, so they do not do both.
The hands clap, so they do not talk and eat.

activities.explanation: The mouth talks and likes to eat, so it does both.

lessons.title: Parts of the Body

activities.prompt: Which body parts will we sing about today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Body Parts in a Song
activities.body: In this lesson, you learn parts of the body from a song. The song names the head, shoulders, knees, and toes. It also names the eyes, ears, mouth, and nose. The song puts eyes and ears together. It puts mouth and nose together.
keyPoints: The song names head, shoulders, knees, and toes.
The song names eyes, ears, mouth, and nose.
Eyes and ears are together in the song.
Mouth and nose are together in the song.
activities.explanation: These are the body parts the song tells you about.

activities.prompt: A child hears the song and wants to remember which body parts go together. Which parts should the child keep as pairs?
steps: The song puts eyes and ears together, so eyes and ears are one pair to remember.
The song puts mouth and nose together, so mouth and nose are another pair to remember.
Therefore, the pairs to remember are eyes with ears and mouth with nose.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which part does the song name?
activities.explanation: The song names shoulders. You can sing about them.

activities.prompt: The song names the nose.
activities.explanation: Yes, the song names the nose.

activities.prompt: The song puts eyes and ______ together.
activities.hint: The song names this part with eyes.
activities.explanation: The song puts eyes and ears together.

activities.prompt: The song puts eyes and mouth together.
activities.explanation: No. The song puts eyes and ears together.

activities.prompt: The song puts mouth and ______ together.
activities.hint: The song names it with mouth.
activities.explanation: The song puts mouth and nose together.

activities.prompt: Riya points to her eyes in the song. Which part does the song put with eyes?
activities.explanation: The song puts eyes and ears together.

activities.prompt: The song puts mouth and nose together. It also puts eyes and ears together.
activities.explanation: Yes, the song puts both of these together.

activities.prompt: The song puts eyes and ears together. A child wants the other pair from the song. Which body parts go together?

why.head and shoulders: Wrong: the child thinks head and shoulders make a song pair.
why.knees and toes: Wrong: the child thinks knees and toes make a song pair.
why.ears and mouth: Wrong: the child mixes ears with mouth from different pairs.

activities.explanation: Right: the song puts mouth and nose together.

activities.prompt: The song puts mouth and nose together. The song puts eyes and ears together. A child puts mouth and ears together and looks sad. What went wrong?
options: The child mixed the song's pairs.
The child kept mouth with nose.
The child kept eyes with ears.
The child put head with shoulders.

Wrong: mouth with nose is a correct song pair.
Wrong: eyes with ears is a correct song pair.
Wrong: the child guesses another mix, not the story's mix.

activities.explanation: Right: mouth and ears come from different song pairs.

lessons.title: Let us Speak

activities.prompt: What can our hands, feet, eyes, and ears help us do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Speak and Name
activities.body: We can speak about our body parts. We use hands for clapping and feet for tapping. Our eyes help us look, and our legs help us walk. Neha and Nitin also speak about their body parts. Neha names her nose, mouth, hands, and legs. Nitin names his shoulders and ears.
keyPoints: We use body parts for actions.
Neha names her body parts.
Nitin names his body parts.
activities.explanation: You can talk about body parts clearly.

activities.prompt: Neha wants a sound from her hands. What can she do?
steps: Neha does not tap, because her feet tap, not her hands.
Her hands are used for clapping, because hands clap.
Her feet are used for tapping, because feet tap.
So she can clap her hands, because clapping uses hands.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which body part do we use for clapping?
activities.explanation: Yes. The hands are used for clapping.

activities.prompt: The feet are used for tapping.
activities.explanation: Yes. The feet are used for tapping.

activities.prompt: Match each body part with what it is used for.
activities.explanation: Hands clap, feet tap, eyes look, and legs walk.

activities.prompt: Who says these are his shoulders?
activities.explanation: Nitin says these are his shoulders.

activities.prompt: Nitin says this is his nose.
activities.explanation: Neha says this is her nose.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order to make a true sentence.
activities.explanation: The sentence is: Nitin says these are his shoulders.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is true?
options: Nitin says these are his legs.
Neha says these are his legs.
Neha says these are her legs.
Nitin says this is her mouth.
activities.explanation: Neha says these are her legs.

activities.prompt: Neha puts her hands together. She wants to make a sound. What will she do?

why.tap with her feet: Wrong: Feet are used for tapping, not clapping.
why.look with her eyes: Wrong: Eyes are used for looking, not clapping.
why.walk with her legs: Wrong: Legs are used for walking, not clapping.

activities.explanation: Right: Hands are used for clapping.

activities.prompt: Neha says, 'This is my mouth.' She asks Nitin to see it. What will Nitin use?

why.his hands for clapping: Wrong: Hands are used for clapping, not looking.
why.his feet for tapping: Wrong: Feet are used for tapping, not looking.
why.his legs for walking: Wrong: Legs are used for walking, not looking.

activities.explanation: Right: Eyes are used for looking at the mouth.

lessons.title: Let us Read and Wash Hands

activities.prompt: What fun story can help our hands get nice and clean?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Senses and Hand Steps
activities.body: Your eyes see. Your ears hear. Your nose smells. Your mouth eats. Your skin feels. For the hand steps, open the tap. Pour water. Water is on your hands. Then your hands are rinsed again. These are the senses in this lesson. The steps use the tap and water.
keyPoints: Eyes see and ears hear.
The nose smells and the mouth eats.
Open the tap, pour water, and rinse the hands again.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows senses and hand steps.

activities.prompt: A child wants water on the hands. The tap can be opened. Water can be poured. What can the child do?
steps: The child opens the tap because the tap can be opened.
The child pours water because water can be poured.
Water is on the hands because the child poured it on them.
The child rinses the hands again because the hands are rinsed again.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which body part helps you see?
activities.explanation: The eyes see. They help you look.

activities.prompt: The nose helps you hear.
activities.explanation: The nose smells. The ears hear.

activities.prompt: The ______ smells.
activities.hint: You use it to smell.
activities.explanation: The nose smells.

activities.prompt: Match each body part to what it does.
activities.explanation: Your eyes see. Your ears hear. Your mouth eats. Your skin feels.

activities.prompt: What do you do first to get water on your hands?
activities.explanation: The tap can be opened. Then water can be poured.

activities.prompt: The hands are ______ again.
activities.hint: It is what happens after water is on the hands.
activities.explanation: The hands are rinsed again.

activities.prompt: The eyes see. A child wants to read. The child covers the eyes. Why is reading hard?

This mixes up seeing with hearing.
This mixes up seeing with smelling.
This mixes up seeing with eating.

activities.explanation: The eyes see, so covered eyes cannot see the words.

activities.prompt: The nose smells. A child knows the food's smell. Which body part helped?

The ears hear sounds, not smells.
The eyes see things, not smells.
The mouth eats food, not smells.

activities.explanation: The nose smells, so it tells the child the smell.

lessons.title: Alphabet Song

activities.prompt: What happy surprise will we find in our alphabet song today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Alphabet Song
activities.body: This lesson is about the Alphabet Song. The song has the letters A, B and C. It also has X, Y and Z. It says sugar is on bread. It says next day morning and come to me. It says we will learn the A B C. It says happy, happy we shall be when we know the A B C.
keyPoints: The song has A, B, C and X, Y, Z.
It says sugar is on bread.
It says happy, happy we shall be.
activities.explanation: These are the main words and ideas in the song.

activities.prompt: You hear the Alphabet Song say sugar is on bread. It says, 'Next day morning, come to me.' It says we shall be happy when we know A B C. You wonder why the song wants you to come.
steps: The song says sugar is on bread, so sugar sits on bread.
The song says come to me, so it asks you to come.
It says next day morning, so it gives a time.
Learning A B C makes us happy, so you come to learn.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In the song, which letter comes with A and B?
activities.explanation: The song says the A B C. So C comes with A and B.

activities.prompt: The song says sugar is on ______.
activities.hint: It is something you eat.
activities.explanation: The song says sugar is on bread.

activities.prompt: Match the parts from the song.
activities.explanation: These pairs show how the song joins its words.

activities.prompt: Put the letters in the order the song says them.
activities.explanation: The song says the A B C in that order.

activities.prompt: What does the song say we will learn?
activities.explanation: The song says we will learn the A B C.

activities.prompt: The song says happy, happy we shall ______.
activities.hint: It is a short word.
activities.explanation: The song says happy, happy we shall be when we know the A B C.

activities.prompt: The Alphabet Song says, 'Next day morning, come to me.' It then says, 'We will learn the A B C.' Why does the song ask you to come?
options: to learn A, B and C
to sing X, Y and Z

why.to eat sugar on bread: Sugar on bread is a song picture, not the reason to come.
why.to sing X, Y and Z: X, Y and Z are song letters, not the reason to come.
why.to wait for the morning: Morning tells when to come, not why to come.

activities.explanation: The song calls you to learn the A B C.

activities.prompt: The Alphabet Song says, 'Next day morning, come to me.' You hear this today. When does the song ask you to come?

why.in the morning before today: The morning before today is the past, not the next day.
why.at night after today: After today at night is not morning.
why.at night before today: Before today at night is not next day morning.

activities.explanation: Next day morning means the morning after today.

activities.prompt: The Alphabet Song has the letters A, B and C. The song also has the letters X, Y and Z. What do both letter groups show about the song?

Sugar and bread are not the letter groups.
Next day morning is not a letter group.
Happy is a feeling word, not a letter group.

activities.explanation: A, B, C and X, Y, Z are letters in the song.

lessons.title: Phonics and Letter Sounds

activities.prompt: What fun sounds do letters make at the start of words?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Letter Sounds
activities.body: Every letter has a sound. We hear that sound at the start of some words. For example, the letter a is for ant. The letter b is for bag. When you say a word, listen to its first sound. That is called the initial sound. Each word has an initial sound.
keyPoints: Each letter has a sound.
The first sound of a word is its initial sound.
a is for ant, b is for bag, c is for cat.
activities.explanation: Listen carefully to the first sound of each word.

activities.prompt: A child sees an ant and a bag. The child wants the card for the ant. Which card fits?
steps: The letter a is for ant.
So the ant's initial sound goes with a.
The letter b is for bag.
So the a card fits ant, not bag.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word starts with the letter 'c'?
activities.explanation: The letter c is for cat. The first sound of cat is /c/.

activities.prompt: The letter 'd' is for dog.
activities.explanation: Yes, the letter d is for dog. The first sound is /d/.

activities.prompt: The letter 'e' is for ______.
activities.hint: It is oval and we eat it.
activities.explanation: The letter e is for egg. The first sound is /e/.

activities.prompt: Match each letter to its word.
activities.explanation: Each letter has a word that starts with its sound.

activities.prompt: Which word starts with the letter 'h'?
activities.explanation: Hut starts with the letter h. The first sound is /h/.

activities.prompt: The word 'ice-cube' starts with the letter 'i'.
activities.explanation: Yes, ice-cube starts with i. The first sound is /i/.

activities.prompt: The initial sound of 'jug' is the letter ______.
activities.hint: It is the first letter of the word.
activities.explanation: The word jug starts with the letter j. That is its initial sound.

activities.prompt: Which letter is the initial sound of the word 'goat'?
activities.explanation: The word goat starts with the letter g. The initial sound is /g/.

activities.prompt: A child wants the card for the ant. The child picks the i card. The teacher says, 'Look again.' Why does the teacher say that?
options: The i card fits the ant, not the ice-cube.
The a card fits the ice-cube, not the ant.
The i card fits the ice-cube, not the ant.
The i card fits the egg, not the ant.

why.The i card fits the ant, not the ice-cub: The i card is for ice-cube, not ant.
why.The a card fits the ice-cube, not the an: The a card is for ant, not ice-cube.
The i card is for ice-cube, not egg.

activities.explanation: The i card fits ice-cube because i is for ice-cube.

activities.prompt: The song has clapping. What should I do with my hands?

The nose smells, so smelling is not for hands.
Legs walk, so walking is not for hands.
The mouth talks, so talking is not for hands.

activities.explanation: Hands clap, so clapping fits the hands.

activities.context: The song has clapping and tapping. I hear it. My head moves. My eyes look around. My hands clap. My legs walk. My nose smells and breathes. My mouth likes to eat. My mouth talks. My little body belongs to me.
activities.prompt: My mouth likes to eat. If I want to eat, what should I do?
options: Use the part that can eat.
Use the part that can hear.
Use the part that can look.
Use the part that can walk.

Ears hear any sound, not eat.

activities.explanation: The mouth likes to eat, so eating uses the mouth.

activities.prompt: Explain why the nose is used for smelling and breathing.
activities.answer: The nose smells and breathes. The eyes look around, the ears hear any sound, and the mouth likes to eat and talks. So the nose is the part that smells and breathes.
points: The nose smells.
The nose breathes.
Other parts have other actions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child sings the body-part song. The song names the head. The song names the shoulders. The song names the knees. The song names the toes. The song names the eyes. The song names the ears. The song names the mouth. The song names the nose. The song puts eyes and ears together. The song puts mouth and nose together. The child stops to think.
activities.prompt: The child wants to show the part where the song puts eyes and ears together. What should the child do?

The song does not join eyes with mouth.
The song does not join ears with nose.
The song does not join head with knees.

activities.explanation: The song joins eyes with ears.

activities.context: A child sings the body-part song. The song names the head. The song names the shoulders. The song names the knees. The song names the toes. The song names the eyes. The song names the ears. The song names the mouth. The song names the nose. The song puts eyes and ears together. The song puts mouth and nose together. The child stops to think.
activities.prompt: The child changes the pair and shows eyes with mouth. What is the problem?
options: The song names only a single part from those parts.
The song leaves those parts out.
The song does not join those parts.

The song joins eyes with ears, not eyes with mouth.
why.The song names only a single part from t: The song names eyes and mouth.
The song names eyes and mouth.

activities.explanation: Eyes go with ears, and mouth goes with nose in the song.

activities.prompt: How does the song help the child follow the joined parts?
activities.answer: The song names the head, shoulders, knees, toes, eyes, ears, mouth, and nose. It puts eyes and ears together. It puts mouth and nose together. The child can sing the joined parts to follow the song.
points: The song names the body parts.
The song puts eyes and ears together.
The song puts mouth and nose together.
The child sings the joined parts to follow the song.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Neha says this is her nose. Nitin says these are his shoulders. Neha says this is her mouth. Nitin says these are his ears. Neha says these are her hands. Neha says these are her legs. The hands are used for clapping. The feet are used for tapping. The eyes are used for looking. The legs are used for walking.
activities.prompt: Neha says these are her hands. If she wants to clap, what should she do?
options: use the parts she named for clapping
use the parts she named for walking
use the parts she named for looking
use the parts she named for tapping

why.use the parts she named for walking: Walking belongs with legs in the facts.
why.use the parts she named for looking: Looking belongs with eyes in the facts.
why.use the parts she named for tapping: Tapping belongs with feet in the facts.

activities.explanation: Neha named her hands, and hands are for clapping.

activities.context: Neha says this is her nose. Nitin says these are his shoulders. Neha says this is her mouth. Nitin says these are his ears. Neha says these are her hands. Neha says these are her legs. The hands are used for clapping. The feet are used for tapping. The eyes are used for looking. The legs are used for walking.
activities.prompt: Neha says these are her legs. If Neha did not use those parts, which action from the case would she not do?

why.clap: The hands are used for clapping.
why.tap: The feet are used for tapping.
why.look: The eyes are used for looking.

activities.explanation: The legs are used for walking.

activities.prompt: Explain why Neha would use her hands when she wants to clap.
activities.answer: Neha says these are her hands. The hands are used for clapping. So when Neha wants to clap, she uses her hands. The feet are used for tapping, the eyes for looking, and the legs for walking.
points: Neha says these are her hands.
The hands are used for clapping.
When she wants to clap, she uses her hands.
Other uses in the facts are tapping, looking, and walking.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the child can feel the water on the hands.
activities.answer: The skin feels. Water is on the hands, so the skin feels the water. The eyes see and the ears hear, but the skin is the part that feels the water.
points: Says the skin feels.
Says water is on the hands.
Links skin feeling to the water on the hands.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the song can make the student happy.
activities.answer: The song says happy, happy we shall be when we know the A B C. So the student can be happy because the song joins happiness with knowing the A B C.
points: Song says happy, happy we shall be.
Song says when we know the A B C.
Happiness is joined to knowing the A B C.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child is matching an ant, a bag, a cat, a dog, an egg, a fish, a goat, a hut, an ice-cube and a jug to initial sounds. The child must give each one its initial sound. The child starts with the cat.
activities.prompt: The child starts with the cat. Which initial sound should the child match to the cat?

why.a: a is for ant, not cat.
why.b: b is for bag, not cat.
why.d: d is for dog, not cat.

activities.explanation: c is for cat, so the cat gets c.

activities.context: A child is matching an ant, a bag, a cat, a dog, an egg, a fish, a goat, a hut, an ice-cube and a jug to initial sounds. The child must give each one its initial sound. The child starts with the cat.
activities.prompt: The child says the jug has the initial sound b. What should the child do to correct the match?

b is for bag, not jug.
g is for goat, not jug.
h is for hut, not jug.

activities.explanation: j is for jug, so the jug gets j.

activities.prompt: Explain why the letter b matches the bag.
activities.answer: The bag begins with the b sound. The fact says b is for bag. So the bag gets b when matching an initial sound. This works because each word has an initial sound.
points: bag begins with b
b is for bag
words have an initial sound
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

lessons.title: Greetings

activities.prompt: What special words can we say when we meet someone or go to bed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Greetings for the Day
activities.body: A greeting is a kind way to welcome someone. In the morning, say Good morning. In the afternoon, say Good afternoon. In the evening, say Good evening. At bedtime, say Good night. When you meet someone, you can also say Namaste.
keyPoints: Say Namaste when you meet someone.
Use Good morning, Good afternoon or Good evening for those times.
Say Good night at bedtime.
activities.explanation: These greetings help you be kind and clear.

activities.prompt: You meet someone in the evening. Later, you go to bed. How do you choose between Good evening and Good night?
steps: At the meeting, say Good evening, because it is the evening greeting.
You are meeting someone, so this is not bedtime.
At bedtime, say Good night, because it is said at bedtime.
So use Good evening at the meeting and Good night at bedtime.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: When you meet someone in the morning, what do you say?
activities.explanation: Good morning is the greeting for the morning.

activities.prompt: Namaste is a greeting used when meeting someone.
activities.explanation: Yes, Namaste is a greeting for meeting someone.

activities.prompt: When I go to bed, I say Good ______.
activities.hint: It is the greeting for bedtime.
activities.explanation: Good night is said at bedtime.

activities.prompt: Match each greeting to its time.
activities.explanation: Each greeting fits its own time of day.

activities.prompt: You meet a friend in the evening. What do you say?
activities.explanation: Good evening is the greeting for the evening.

activities.prompt: You say Good morning when you go to bed.
activities.explanation: Good morning is for the morning. At bedtime, you say Good night.

activities.prompt: Put these greetings in order from morning to bedtime.
activities.explanation: The day moves from morning to afternoon, then evening, then bedtime.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
options: I say Good night in the morning.
I say Good morning in the morning.
I say Good afternoon at bedtime.
I say Good evening in the morning.
activities.explanation: Good morning is the greeting for the morning. The other greetings do not match their times.

activities.prompt: A story says, 'The child met a friend and said, Good morning.' What does this line tell us?
options: The meeting is in the afternoon.
The meeting is in the morning.
The meeting is in the evening.

This confuses morning with the afternoon greeting.
This confuses morning with the bedtime greeting.
This confuses morning with the evening greeting.

activities.explanation: Good morning is the greeting for the morning.

activities.prompt: A child says, 'Namaste' to someone. What does this show?
options: The child is going to bed now.
The meeting must be in the morning.
The meeting must be in the evening.
The child is meeting someone now.

This confuses Namaste with the bedtime greeting.
This adds a morning time that Namaste does not show.
This adds an evening time that Namaste does not show.

activities.explanation: Namaste is a greeting used when meeting someone.

lessons.title: Actions and letters

activities.prompt: What fun actions and letters will we discover today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Action words and letters
activities.body: An action word tells what someone does. You can say, 'I comb my hair.' You can say, 'I walk to school.' Your book shows actions like see, eat and hear. You also meet letters like G and H. You meet small letters like f and g. Lowercase letters are small letters. Look at each letter and the words that start with it.
keyPoints: Action words tell what someone does.
You can comb your hair and walk to school.
The letters G, H, I, J and K are shown.
The letters f, g, h, i and j are lowercase.
activities.explanation: Action words and letters help you read the sentences in your book.

activities.prompt: A child sees big letters G, H, I, J and K. The child sees small letters f, g, h, i and j. Which big letters have a small partner shown?
steps: G has a partner because big G and small g match.
H has a partner because big H and small h match.
I and J have partners because small i and j are shown.
K has no partner because no small k is shown.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which sentence tells about hearing?
activities.explanation: The sentence says 'I hear the bell ring.' Hear is the action.

activities.prompt: I ______ my food.
activities.hint: It starts with e.
activities.explanation: The lesson says 'I eat my food.' Eat tells what you do.

activities.prompt: Match each sentence with its action word.
activities.explanation: Each sentence has an action word. Comb, eat, hear and walk tell what you do.

activities.prompt: Which word starts with the letter f?
activities.explanation: Fox starts with the letter f. The other words start with other letters.

activities.prompt: Put these letters in the order shown in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The letters are shown in this order: G, H, I, J, K.

activities.prompt: Which word starts with the small letter j?
activities.explanation: The small letter j is shown. Jug starts with j.

activities.prompt: A child walks to school. The child uses a body part to step. Which shown word names it?

why.fish: A fish swims in water, not for stepping.
why.girl: A girl is a child, not a body part.
why.goat: A goat is an animal, not a body part.

activities.explanation: A foot helps a child step when walking.

activities.prompt: A child sees big letters G, H, I, J, K. The child sees small letters f, g, h, i, j. Which big letter has no small partner shown?

why.G: G has small g shown, so it has a partner.
why.H: H has small h shown, so it has a partner.
why.I: I has small i shown, so it has a partner.

activities.explanation: K is shown big, but no small k is shown.

activities.prompt: A child sees Ll, Mm, Nn, Oo and P. The child looks for the letter after Nn. Which letter comes next?

why.Ll: Ll comes before Nn, not after it.
why.Mm: Mm comes before Nn, not after it.
why.Nn: Nn is the same letter, not after it.

activities.explanation: Oo comes right after Nn in the shown list.

lessons.title: Hop a Little

activities.prompt: What playful moves will our happy rhyme teach us today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Hop a Little
activities.body: Hop a Little is a rhyme. It tells you to hop, jump, stamp, skip and tap. It says to tap one knee. It uses the numbers one, two and three. It also says to dance, twist, shake your hand and yawn. It tells you to sleep a little in your bed.
keyPoints: The rhyme tells you to hop, jump, stamp, skip and tap.
It says to tap one knee and shake your hand.
It uses one, two and three and says to sleep in your bed.
activities.explanation: These are the words and actions in the rhyme.

activities.prompt: A child hears 'tap one knee' and taps the floor. Why is this not following the rhyme?
steps: The rhyme says to tap one knee.
The line names a knee, so tap a knee.
The floor is not named in that line.
So the child should tap one knee, not the floor.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The rhyme tells you to hop a little.
activities.explanation: Yes, hopping is one of the actions in the rhyme.

activities.prompt: Which action does the rhyme tell you to do with your hand?
activities.explanation: The rhyme says to shake your hand.

activities.prompt: Match each action to the words that go with it in the rhyme.
activities.explanation: The rhyme joins these actions with these words.

activities.prompt: The rhyme says to tap one ______.
activities.hint: Use the word from the rhyme that follows 'tap one'.
activities.explanation: The rhyme says to tap one knee.

activities.prompt: What does the rhyme say to shake?
activities.explanation: The rhyme says to shake your hand.

activities.prompt: The rhyme tells you to tap two knees.
activities.explanation: It says to tap one knee, not two.

activities.prompt: Put the numbers from the rhyme in order, from first to last.
activities.explanation: The rhyme has the numbers one, two and three.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is true about the rhyme?
options: It says to tap two knees.
It says to shake your bed.
It says to tap one knee.
It says to sleep in your hand.
activities.explanation: The rhyme says to tap one knee.

activities.prompt: The rhyme says, 'jump a little.' A child jumps many times. What did the child forget?

why.to sleep in a bed: Sleeping in bed is a different line, so it does not fit.
why.to shake your hand: Shaking a hand is a different line, so it does not fit.
why.to tap one knee: Tapping one knee is a different line, so it does not fit.

activities.explanation: The rhyme says jump a little, so many jumps do not fit.

activities.prompt: The rhyme says, 'dance a little.' A child dances, then stops. Why stop?
options: to dance for a long time

why.to dance for a long time: A long dance is not a little dance.
why.to sleep in bed: Sleeping in bed is a different line.
why.to tap one knee: Tapping one knee is a different line.

activities.explanation: The rhyme says dance a little, so stopping fits.

lessons.title: Actions in pictures

activities.prompt: What are the people and animals doing in these pictures?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Look at the action
activities.body: A picture can show an action. Look at who is in the picture. Then look at what the person or animal is doing. The lesson gives picture sentences. They say dancing, jumping, yawning, hopping, walking, running, stretching, sleeping, bending and skipping. Read the action word at the end.
keyPoints: A picture sentence tells what someone is doing.
The doing word is the action word.
Read the whole sentence to check.
activities.explanation: Look at the picture and find the action word.

activities.prompt: A child sees a picture sentence. It says the dog is sleeping. What should the child picture?
steps: First, find who the sentence tells about: the dog.
Next, find the action word: sleeping.
The fact joins the dog and sleeping in one sentence.
So the child should picture the dog sleeping.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the dog doing in the picture sentence?
activities.explanation: The picture sentence says the dog is sleeping.

activities.prompt: The picture sentence says Seema is running.
activities.explanation: It says Seema is running.

activities.prompt: The picture sentence says Vittal is ______.
activities.hint: It starts with b.
activities.explanation: The picture sentence says Vittal is bending.

activities.prompt: Match each person or animal to the action.
activities.explanation: Match each one to the action said in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which picture sentence is about walking?
activities.explanation: The lesson says they are walking.

activities.prompt: The picture sentence says Kumar is sleeping.
activities.explanation: The lesson says Kumar is stretching.

activities.prompt: Which pair has two correct picture sentences?
options: Seema is stretching. / Kumar is running.
Vittal is sleeping. / The dog is bending.
The boy is dancing. / The dog is walking.
Seema is running. / Kumar is stretching.
activities.explanation: Seema is running and Kumar is stretching in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order to make the picture sentence about the dog.
activities.explanation: The picture sentence says the dog is sleeping.

activities.prompt: A picture sentence says they are dancing. Why might they move?
activities.explanation: Dancing is often done for fun, so this fits.

activities.prompt: A picture sentence says the boy is skipping. How might he feel?

This mistakes skipping for feeling scared.
This mistakes skipping for feeling angry.
This mistakes skipping for feeling sleepy.

activities.explanation: Skipping often goes with happy feelings, so this fits.

lessons.title: Family and The Sparrow Family

activities.prompt: Who will we meet in this warm family story?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Family and the Sparrow Family
activities.body: A family can play, eat, dance, sing and read together. The song asks Mother to play. It asks Father to eat. Brother and sister are asked to dance. Grandmother is asked to sing. Grandfather is asked to read. The reply is, "Yes, I shall." The song says, "We are a family!" Mama and Papa sparrow were making a nest.
keyPoints: The song names Mother, Father, Brother and sister, Grandmother and Grandfather.
The reply in the song is 'Yes, I shall.'
Mama and Papa sparrow were making a nest.
activities.explanation: The song shows a family doing things together.

activities.prompt: The song asks many family people to do things together. Why does it end with 'We are a family!'?
steps: Mother says, 'Yes, I shall,' because she agrees to play.
The song asks Father to eat, because eating together is family time.
Brother, sister, Grandmother, and Grandfather join in, because family shares.
So 'We are a family!' fits because these people do things together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Sparrow Family
activities.body: A nest is the safe, soft place Mama and Papa sparrow were making. They found a safe place. The nest was soft and warm. Mama sparrow laid three small eggs. Then three little heads popped out. The sparrow family had a safe, warm nest.
keyPoints: A nest is the safe, soft place the sparrow family was making.
Mama sparrow laid three small eggs.
Three little heads popped out.
activities.explanation: The sparrow family's nest is safe and warm.

activities.prompt: What were Mama and Papa sparrow making?
activities.explanation: They were making a nest in a safe place.

activities.prompt: In the song, Father is asked to read with me.
activities.explanation: The song asks Father to eat with me. Grandfather is asked to read.

activities.prompt: Match each family member to the action in the song.
activities.explanation: The song gives each family member a different action.

activities.prompt: What does the song say about the family?
activities.explanation: The song says, 'We are a family!'

activities.prompt: Mama sparrow laid three small eggs, and then three little heads popped out.
activities.explanation: The lesson says three small eggs were laid, then three little heads popped out.

activities.prompt: Put the family members in the order the song calls them.
activities.explanation: The song calls Mother, Father, Brother and sister, Grandmother, then Grandfather.

activities.prompt: A child asks Mother to play. Mother says, 'Yes, I shall.' What will happen next?

Read is not what Mother was asked to do here.
Sing is not what Mother was asked to do here.
Dance is not what Mother was asked to do here.

activities.explanation: Mother says yes to play, so they will play together.

activities.prompt: Mama and Papa sparrow make a nest. They find a safe place. Mama sparrow lays three small eggs. Why is a safe place good?

This thinks a safe place is for noise.
This ignores that the nest is warm, not cold.
This thinks eggs need to roll far, not stay safe.

activities.explanation: The place is safe, so it helps the eggs stay safe.

lessons.title: Letter sounds and alphabet

activities.prompt: What sounds do letters make when we read and sing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Letter sounds and the alphabet
activities.body: Some words begin with the same sound. The word father begins with the f sound. Fox, feather, food, foot, five and flag also begin with f. The word mother begins with the m sound. Man, mask, mouse, moon, monkey and mouth also begin with m. The alphabet begins with A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J and K. It ends with W, X, Y and Z.
keyPoints: Father begins with the f sound.
Mother begins with the m sound.
The alphabet begins with A and ends with Z.
activities.explanation: Listen for the first sound in each word.

activities.prompt: A child hears father and fox and asks why these words can go in the same sound group.
steps: The word father begins with the f sound, so it is an f sound word.
The word fox is in the f sound word list, so it also begins with f.
Both words have the f sound at the start, so they match.
The child can put father and fox together because their first sound is the same.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which word begins with the f sound?
activities.explanation: Father begins with the f sound. Mother, monkey and mouth begin with the m sound.

activities.prompt: The word monkey begins with the m sound.
activities.explanation: Monkey is one of the m sound words. It starts with m.

activities.prompt: Match each letter group to its place in the alphabet.
activities.explanation: The alphabet begins with A, B, C. It continues with L, M, N. It ends with W, X, Y and Z.

activities.prompt: Put these letters in alphabet order.
activities.explanation: The alphabet begins with A, B, C, D and E.

activities.prompt: Which group shows the alphabet ending?
activities.explanation: The alphabet ends with W, X, Y and Z. The other groups come earlier.

activities.prompt: The word mouse begins with the f sound.
activities.explanation: Mouse begins with the m sound. Fox begins with the f sound.

activities.prompt: The alphabet ends with W, X, Y and ______.
activities.hint: It is the last letter.
activities.explanation: The last letter group is W, X, Y and Z.

activities.prompt: A child hears mother and moon. The child smiles. The child hears father and fox. The child smiles again. Why does the child smile?
options: Both pairs start with the same sound.
Both pairs end with the same sound.
Both pairs have the same middle sound.
Both pairs have the same last letter.

The child is not matching the last sound.
The child is not matching the middle sound.
The child is not matching the last letter.

activities.explanation: Mother and moon start with m; father and fox start with f.

activities.prompt: A child puts letter cards in order. The cards show L, M, N, O. A friend hides the next card. The child needs the hidden card. Which letter is hidden?

why.Q: This skips P, which comes before Q.
why.R: This skips P and Q, which come earlier.
why.V: This jumps far past P to a later letter.

activities.explanation: P comes after O in the alphabet.

options: It matches the time of the meeting.
It matches bedtime rather than the meeting time.
It matches the afternoon rather than the meeting time.
It matches the evening rather than the meeting time.

why.It matches bedtime rather than the meeti: Bedtime words are for going to bed, not for this meeting.
why.It matches the afternoon rather than the: Afternoon words are for the afternoon, not for this meeting.
why.It matches the evening rather than the m: Evening words are for the evening, not for this meeting.

activities.context: In the morning, a child meets someone and says the greeting for the morning. In the afternoon, the child meets someone and says the greeting for the afternoon. In the evening, the child meets someone and says the greeting for the evening. When the child goes to bed, the child says the greeting for bedtime. When the child meets someone, the child also says Namaste.
activities.prompt: If the child in the case met someone in the evening instead of in the morning, what should the child do?
options: Use the words for that time of day.
Use the words for the afternoon.
Use the words for the morning.

Bedtime words fit going to bed, not this meeting.
Afternoon words do not fit the changed meeting time.
Morning words were for the earlier time, not the changed time.

points: Good evening is the greeting for the evening.
Good night is said at bedtime.
Good evening is used when meeting someone in the evening.
Good night is used when going to bed.

why.fish and foot: fish and foot both begin with f, so they match.
why.house and hut: house and hut both begin with h, so they match.

activities.prompt: The child hears the bell ring. If the child does the same action as in I see my teacher, what would the child do next?

why.comb the hair: Combing hair is an action in the case but not the one that matches seeing the teacher.
why.eat the food: Eating food is an action in the case but not the one that matches seeing the teacher.
why.walk to school: Walking to school is an action in the case but not the one that matches seeing the teacher.

activities.prompt: Explain why fish, foot, and fox can be put together on the paper.
activities.answer: They can be put together because each word begins with the letter f. The paper shows the lowercase f and the words fish, foot, and fox. So they match by their first letter.

foot begins with f
fox begins with f
the paper shows lowercase f
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child is learning the rhyme. The child hears that the rhyme tells us to hop a little, jump a little, stamp a little, skip a little, dance a little, twist a little, yawn a little, and sleep a little in your bed. The rhyme has the numbers one, two and three. The rhyme also says to tap one knee and shake your hand. The child practices the new words hop, jump, stamp, skip and tap.
activities.prompt: The child may act out only the new words from the rhyme. Which action should the child choose?

why.do a little twist: Twist is in the rhyme, but it is not one of the new words.
why.shake your hand: Shaking your hand is in the rhyme, but shake is not one of the new words.
why.give a little yawn: Yawn is in the rhyme, but it is not one of the new words.

activities.explanation: Tap is one of the new words; the rhyme says to tap one knee.

activities.context: A child is learning the rhyme. The child hears that the rhyme tells us to hop a little, jump a little, stamp a little, skip a little, dance a little, twist a little, yawn a little, and sleep a little in your bed. The rhyme has the numbers one, two and three. The rhyme also says to tap one knee and shake your hand. The child practices the new words hop, jump, stamp, skip and tap.
activities.prompt: A child hears the rhyme say to tap one knee. If the child follows that part, how many knees should be tapped?

why.two knees: The rhyme says one knee, so two is wrong.
why.three knees: The rhyme says one knee, so three is wrong.
why.no knees: The rhyme says to tap one knee, so no knees is wrong.

activities.explanation: The rhyme says to tap one knee, so just one knee is tapped.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between tapping one knee and shaking your hand in the rhyme?
activities.answer: Tapping one knee is an action in the rhyme, and tap is one of the new words. Shaking your hand is also an action in the rhyme, but shake is not listed as a new word. Each is an action in the rhyme.
points: Tapping one knee is an action in the rhyme.

Shaking your hand is also in the rhyme.
Shake is not listed as a new word.

activities.prompt: Explain why the picture sentence that says the dog is sleeping should not go with a picture of Seema running.
activities.answer: The sentence tells about the dog, not Seema. Sleeping is the dog's action. Running is Seema's action. If the sentence says the dog is sleeping, its picture must show the dog sleeping, not Seema running.
points: Names the dog as the subject.
Names sleeping as the dog's action.
Contrasts it with Seema running.
Says the picture must match the sentence.

activities.context: A child sings the song. The child sings, “Mother, mother, will you play with me?” and hears the reply, “Yes, I shall.” The child then sings, “We are a family!” Next, the child thinks of the sparrow story: Mama and Papa sparrow were making a nest in a safe place, and the nest was soft and warm. activities.body: Once there was a man. He sold caps, so he was a cap-seller. He carried many caps in a basket on his head. One day, he slept under a tree. Monkeys were on the tree. They came down and took all his caps. When he woke up, his basket was empty. The monkeys were wearing his caps.

why.The mango set aside for the bird: That mango is for the bird, which nests on the tree.

activities.context: A traveller is resting under a tree. Five yellow mangoes are hanging on the tree. A bird nests on the tree. A squirrel runs up the tree. A rabbit lives under the tree. why.Give it to the bird: The bird already has its own mango.

The rabbit lives under the tree.
One is resting there and one lives there.
Both are under the same tree.

She is there to sell vegetables.

She is there to grow vegetables.

He grows vegetables.

Mini goes with him and he takes her around.

She wants Father to show her more colourful flowers.
The flowers remind her of what her mother can make.

Father begins to tell the flower names.

She wants to know why she can see apples.

why.She wants to know why she can see apples: This is not right: the apples are already seen; her question is about the large fruits.

activities.title: Foods in a lunch box
activities.body: This lesson shows foods in lunch boxes. One child has poori with aloo sabzi. Another child has roti with sabzi. One child has fruits. One child got idli with chutney. Another has gobhi paratha, and one got Godok. One child has chilla in the box. Poori goes with aloo sabzi, sabzi goes with roti, and idli goes with chutney.
keyPoints: This lesson shows foods in lunch boxes.
Poori goes with aloo sabzi.
Idli goes with chutney.
activities.explanation: Foods in a lunch box can be paired in different ways.

activities.prompt: A child has poori with aloo sabzi. The child asks, 'What goes with poori?'
steps: Poori is eaten with aloo sabzi.
The child has poori with aloo sabzi.
So the child can eat poori and aloo sabzi together.
The answer is aloo sabzi goes with poori.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is idli eaten with?
activities.explanation: Idli is eaten with chutney.

activities.prompt: Poori is eaten with aloo sabzi.
activities.explanation: Poori goes with aloo sabzi.

activities.prompt: Poori is eaten with aloo ______.
activities.hint: It completes the food pair.
activities.explanation: Poori is eaten with aloo sabzi.

activities.prompt: Match each food with what it is eaten with.
activities.explanation: Poori goes with aloo sabzi, sabzi with roti, and idli with chutney.

activities.explanation: Idli is eaten with chutney.

activities.prompt: What can friends do when someone has no lunch?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Food to share
activities.body: In this lesson, the mother is sick. There is no lunch for the speaker. The speaker has no lunch and says so. Someone offers a chilla. Someone offers a paratha. Someone says thank you. This is a lesson about sharing food.
keyPoints: The mother is sick.
There is no lunch for the speaker.
Someone offers a chilla and a paratha.
Someone says thank you.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows food being offered.

activities.prompt: The mother is sick. There is no lunch. Someone offers food. Why does the speaker say thank you?
steps: The mother is sick, so the speaker has no lunch.
Someone says to take the chilla and offers it.
Someone says to have the paratha and offers it.
The speaker says thank you because food is shared when there is no lunch.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why is there no lunch for the speaker?
options: Because the speaker says thank you.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the mother is sick. So there is no lunch for the speaker.

activities.prompt: The speaker says there is no ______.
activities.hint: It is the meal you eat in the day.
activities.explanation: The speaker tells someone there is no lunch.

activities.prompt: Match each beginning with its ending.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows the mother is sick, the speaker has no lunch, a chilla is offered, and someone says thank you.

activities.prompt: Which foods are offered?
activities.explanation: The lesson says a chilla and a paratha are offered.

activities.prompt: Put the story parts in order.
items: There is no lunch for the speaker.
activities.explanation: This is the order of the story in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Which sentence shows sharing food?
activities.explanation: A chilla and a paratha are offered. That is sharing food.

activities.prompt: A child has no lunch. Someone offers a chilla. How does the child likely feel?

why.angry and upset: The child may think an offer is a bad thing.
why.bored and sleepy: The child may not see why food matters.
why.shy and worried: The child may think an offer is scary.

activities.explanation: The offer helps, so the child feels glad and thankful.

activities.prompt: There is no lunch. Someone offers a paratha. The child says thank you. Why?
options: The child is glad for the food.
The child is angry at the offer.
The child has a lot of lunch.
The child does not want food.

The child may think an offer makes people angry.
The child may think lunch is already enough.
The child may think the food is not wanted.

activities.explanation: The child says thank you because the food is given.

activities.prompt: The mother is sick. There is no lunch. What does the speaker need?

why.Someone to hide lunch: Hiding lunch would not give the speaker food.
why.Someone to keep lunch: Keeping lunch would not give the speaker food.
why.Someone to take lunch: Taking lunch would not give the speaker food.

activities.explanation: With no lunch, sharing lunch gives the speaker food.

activities.prompt: The mother is sick. The speaker has no lunch. Someone gives a paratha. Why is this kind?

The child may think lunch is already there.
The child may forget that the mother is sick.
The child may think hiding food is kind.

activities.explanation: The speaker has no lunch, so the food helps.

lessons.title: Milk, curds and butter

activities.prompt: Where do milk, curds and butter come from?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Milk, curds and butter
activities.body: Milk comes from cows. We get milk from cows. Cows give us milk. We make curds from milk. We make butter from milk. Curds are made from milk. Butter is made from milk. Milk is used to make curds and butter. We should say thank you.
keyPoints: We get milk from cows.
We make curds and butter from milk.
We should say thank you.
activities.explanation: Cows give milk. Milk is used to make curds and butter.

activities.prompt: A child sees milk, curds, and butter. The child asks, 'Why do curds and butter go with milk?'
steps: Cows give us milk; that is why we have milk.
Curds are made from milk; that is why curds go with milk.
Butter is made from milk; that is why butter goes with milk.
Milk is used for curds and butter; so say thank you.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do we get from cows?
activities.explanation: Cows give us milk. The lesson says we get milk from cows.

activities.prompt: Curds are made from milk.
activities.explanation: Yes, curds are made from milk. Milk is used to make curds.

activities.prompt: We make butter from ______.
activities.hint: It comes from cows.
activities.explanation: Butter is made from milk. Milk comes from cows.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it does or is made from.
activities.explanation: Cows give milk. Milk is used to make curds and butter.

activities.prompt: What do we use milk to make?
activities.explanation: Milk is used to make curds and butter.

activities.prompt: Milk is made from butter.
activities.explanation: The lesson says butter is made from milk. Milk is not made from butter.

activities.prompt: We should say ______ you.
activities.hint: A kind word.
activities.explanation: We should say thank you. It is kind to say thank you.

activities.prompt: Put these in order, from the cow to the curds.
items: We make curds from the milk.
activities.explanation: Cows give milk. We get milk from cows. Then milk is used to make curds.

activities.prompt: A child drinks milk. The child says, 'Thank you, cow.' Why does the child say this?
options: The child knows cows give us milk.
The child thinks butter comes from cows.
The child thinks milk comes from curds.
The child thinks curds come from cows.

Wrong: butter is made from milk, not cows.
Wrong: milk comes from cows, not curds.
Wrong: curds are made from milk, not cows.

activities.explanation: Right: cows give us milk, so the child says thank you.

activities.prompt: A child has milk. The child asks, 'Can butter be made from this milk?' What is the best answer?
options: Yes, butter is made from milk.
No, butter is made from curds.
No, butter is made from cows.
Yes, curds are made from butter.

Wrong: butter is made from milk, not curds.
Wrong: cows give milk, but butter is made from milk.
Wrong: curds are made from milk, not butter.

activities.explanation: Right: butter is made from milk, so the answer is yes.

activities.title: Colour Words in Sentences

keyPoints: A colour word describes a thing.
You can say “The ___ is ___.”
You can say “There is a ___ ___.”
activities.explanation: Colour words help you describe things clearly.

activities.prompt: The cow is brown.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the cow is brown. Well done.

activities.prompt: What colour is the cap?
activities.explanation: The lesson says the cap is purple.

activities.prompt: There are ______ oranges.
activities.hint: The number comes after “are”.
activities.explanation: The lesson says there are four oranges.

activities.prompt: There is a purple jeep.
activities.explanation: The jeep in the lesson is green. The purple thing is the cap.

activities.prompt: Which sentence tells us about a green jeep?
activities.explanation: The sentence with “green jeep” talks about the jeep. The other sentences talk about a cap, a cow, and oranges.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence about the green jeep.
activities.explanation: The words make the sentence “There is a green jeep.”

activities.prompt: The speaker says, 'The lunch is mine.' What does mine mean here?

A cow cannot own the lunch in these facts.
A cap cannot own the lunch in these facts.
A jeep cannot own the lunch in these facts.

why.the jeeps: The facts give no number for jeeps.

why.the cap: The cap is purple, not green.
why.the lunch: The lunch has no colour in these facts.

activities.explanation: says the jeep is green, so pick the jeep.

activities.prompt: What tasty fruits and vegetables will our riddles help us discover today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Clues for a riddle
activities.body: A riddle gives clues for you to guess. In this lesson, some clues are about a riddle fruit and a riddle vegetable. Look at colour, outside, inside and bunch clues. Read each clue carefully and join the clues that belong together.
keyPoints: The riddle fruit has colour and bunch clues.
The riddle vegetable has colour and crying clues.
Read all clues before you choose.
activities.explanation: Clues help you solve a riddle step by step.

activities.prompt: A child hears two riddles at lunch and mixes up the fruit clue with the vegetable clue. Which clues help sort them out?
steps: The fruit clue says its name is its colour, so that colour word points to the fruit.
The fruit clue also says green or purple and a bunch, so those clues point to the fruit too.
The vegetable clue says pink or white, so those colours point to the vegetable.
The vegetable clue says cutting it makes you cry, so tears point to the vegetable, not the fruit.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The riddle fruit can come in green or purple.
activities.explanation: Yes! Green and purple are the colours given for the riddle fruit.

activities.prompt: What colours can the riddle vegetable be?
activities.explanation: The lesson says the riddle vegetable is pink and may also be white.

activities.prompt: The riddle vegetable makes you ______ if you cut it.
activities.hint: It starts with c.
activities.explanation: That is right. Cutting the riddle vegetable can make you cry.

activities.prompt: Match each clue to its ending.
activities.explanation: Well done! You matched each clue to its ending.

activities.prompt: Which two clues both tell about the riddle fruit?
options: It is pink in colour. It may be white too.
It comes in a bunch. It is green or purple.
It is hard and brown outside. It is soft inside.
It may be white. It makes you cry.

why.They want to watch flowers bloom every d: Flowers blooming is a spring fact, not the reason for a pool dip.

activities.context: Children are in spring. They play. Flowers bloom in spring. Flowers bloom every day. Then it is summer. Summer is hot. People want to stay cool. Everyone wants a dip in the pool. The pool is a place for a dip. People dip in the pool to feel cool.

The sun's rays are enjoyed on sunny days.

why.Give it to her grandparents because they: Her grandparents living there does not make the frock theirs to take.
why.Leave it because her family is visiting: The family visit does not make leaving the frock the right choice.

activities.explanation: A cotton frock suits the hot place, so wearing it makes sense.

activities.title: Rain, Sleep and Waking

Rain was coming down outside.
Anandi's dream was about rainbows.
Anandi woke and looked out her window.

activities.prompt: Why did Anandi get up to look outside after waking?
steps: Rain was coming down outside, so Anandi had rain to look at.
Anandi was in deep sleep, so she was not awake yet.
Anandi woke from sleep, so she could get up.
She got up to look outside, so waking let her see rain.

activities.title: Anandi's Actions
activities.body: Anandi was in deep sleep. She was seeing a dream. Her dream was about rainbows. Then she woke from sleep. She got up to look outside. She looked out through her window. The rain was coming down outside. Anandi looked out.
keyPoints: Anandi slept deeply.
She dreamed about rainbows.
She woke and looked outside.
Rain was coming down.
activities.explanation: The lesson tells us what Anandi did.

activities.prompt: What was Anandi doing at the start of the lesson?
activities.explanation: The lesson says Anandi was sleeping deeply.

activities.prompt: Anandi was sleeping deeply.
activities.explanation: Yes, the lesson tells us Anandi was in deep sleep.

activities.explanation: The lesson says Anandi's dream was about rainbows.

activities.explanation: The lesson says Anandi got up to look outside.

activities.prompt: Anandi looked out through her door.
activities.explanation: The lesson says she looked out through her window, not her door.

activities.explanation: Right: the dream came before she woke.

lessons.title: Colouring the Flowers

activities.prompt: Which pretty colours will Anandi use for her flowers today?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Colours for a Picture
activities.body: Anandi put colours on flowers. She used violet, indigo, blue, orange and red for flowers. She used green for the leaves. She did not use yellow for a flower. She saved yellow for the Sun. The Sun could look bright and cheerful. Indigo is one of the rainbow colours.
keyPoints: Anandi put colours on flowers.
Green was for the leaves, and yellow was saved for the Sun.
Indigo is one of the rainbow colours.
activities.explanation: The lesson shows which colours Anandi used.

activities.prompt: Why did Anandi save yellow for the Sun?
steps: Anandi did not use yellow for a flower.
She saved yellow for the Sun instead.
The Sun could look bright and cheerful.
So she saved yellow to keep the Sun bright and cheerful.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Anandi used green for the leaves.
activities.explanation: Yes. Green was the colour used for the leaves.

activities.prompt: What did Anandi save yellow for?
activities.explanation: Yellow was saved for the Sun. The Sun could look bright and cheerful.

activities.prompt: Anandi used ______ for the leaves.
activities.hint: Think of the colour of leaves in the picture.
activities.explanation: Green was the colour Anandi used for the leaves.

activities.prompt: Match each colour to what Anandi used it for.
activities.explanation: Violet and indigo were used for flowers. Green was for the leaves. Yellow was saved for the Sun.

activities.prompt: Anandi used yellow for one flower.
activities.explanation: No. Anandi did not use yellow for a flower. She saved it for the Sun.

activities.prompt: Anandi saved yellow for the Sun. What could the Sun look like?
activities.explanation: The lesson says the Sun could look bright and cheerful. Yellow was saved for the Sun.

activities.prompt: Put the words in order to make a sentence from the lesson.
activities.explanation: The sentence is: Anandi saved yellow for the Sun.

activities.prompt: Which colour did Anandi use for a flower?
activities.explanation: Indigo was used for another flower. Green was for leaves, and yellow was saved for the Sun.

activities.prompt: Anandi colours the leaves green. She does not use yellow for a flower. She saves yellow for the Sun. What is her plan?
options: She plans a colour for each part.
She plans to hide all the colours.
She plans to use yellow on leaves.
She plans to forget the flowers.

She uses colours; she does not hide them.
Leaves are green, so yellow is not for leaves.
She colours flowers, so she does not forget them.

activities.explanation: She chooses green leaves and keeps yellow for the Sun.

lessons.title: The Yellow Sun and the Gone Rainbow

activities.prompt: What happened when the yellow sun met the rainbow in the garden?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Yellow Sun and the Gone Rainbow
activities.body: The Sun was up in the sky. It was giving light and had a yellow shine. Lovely flowers covered the garden. The garden had lovely flowers all over it. The rainbow disappeared after colouring the flowers and the Sun. The flowers still looked lovely.
keyPoints: The Sun was up in the sky and gave light.
The Sun had a yellow shine.
The rainbow disappeared after colouring the flowers and the Sun.
activities.explanation: This card helps you remember what the lesson says.

activities.prompt: The rainbow is gone. Why can the flowers and Sun still look lovely and yellow?
steps: The rainbow disappeared after it coloured the flowers.
The lovely flowers stayed all over the garden.
The rainbow disappeared after it coloured the Sun.
So the garden and sky stayed lovely and yellow.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which thing had a yellow shine?
activities.explanation: The lesson says the Sun had a yellow shine.

activities.prompt: The Sun was up in the sky.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the Sun was up in the sky.

activities.prompt: The rainbow ______ after colouring the flowers and the Sun.
activities.hint: It was no longer seen.
activities.explanation: The lesson says the rainbow disappeared after colouring the flowers and the Sun.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Check each thing with the words the lesson uses for it.

activities.prompt: What disappeared after colouring the flowers and the Sun?
activities.explanation: The lesson says the rainbow disappeared after colouring the flowers and the Sun.

activities.prompt: Lovely flowers ______ the garden.
activities.hint: They were all over it.
activities.explanation: The lesson says lovely flowers covered the garden.

activities.prompt: You see a garden after the rainbow is gone. Lovely flowers are all over it. Why does it still look lovely?
options: The lovely flowers are still there.
The rainbow is still in the garden.
The Sun has become a flower.
The garden has no flowers now.

This thinks the rainbow stayed after it disappeared.
This confuses the Sun with a flower.
This thinks the flowers vanished too.

activities.explanation: The flowers stayed and kept the garden lovely.

activities.prompt: You see flowers all over a garden. They make the garden beautiful. What does lovely mean here?

This thinks lovely means hard to find.
This thinks lovely is a loud sound.
This thinks lovely is dark like night.

activities.explanation: Lovely flowers look very pretty.

activities.context: Rain was coming down outside. Anandi was in deep sleep. In her sleep she was seeing a dream. Her dream was about rainbows. Then Anandi woke from sleep. She got up to look outside. She looked out through her window. There was rain outside.
activities.prompt: If Anandi had stayed in deep sleep, what would she not have done?

The case says she had a dream about rainbows while asleep.
Deep sleep is the state she would have stayed in.
The rainbow dream was part of her sleep.

activities.explanation: Going to the window came after she woke from sleep.

activities.context: Rain was coming down outside. Anandi was in deep sleep. In her sleep she was seeing a dream. Her dream was about rainbows. Then Anandi woke from sleep. She got up to look outside. She looked out through her window. There was rain outside.
activities.prompt: After waking, what should Anandi do to find out if rain is outside?
options: Go to the window and look.
Stay in bed with her eyes closed.

Deep sleep would not show her the rain outside.
A dream is not the same as looking outside.
Staying in bed would not help her look through the window.

activities.explanation: Looking through the window lets her check outside.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between Anandi in deep sleep and Anandi after she wakes?
activities.answer: In deep sleep, Anandi has a dream about rainbows. After she wakes, she rises and goes to the window. She looks out, and rain is falling outside.
points: In deep sleep, Anandi has a dream about rainbows.
After waking, Anandi rises.
Anandi goes to the window and looks out.
Rain is falling outside.
